facts.fact_text: According to the applicants, in the period from 20 May to 6 July 2010 they participated in protest activities against a road-construction project in Gorky Park (Парк ім. Горького) in Kharkiv.
According to the applicants, the protest activities in Gorky Park included obstructing tree-felling work.
Tree felling commenced on 20 May 2010 in Gorky Park, attracting a number of individuals who protested against it, including, according to the applicants, the applicants themselves.
According to the applicants, there were hundreds of protesters at Gorky Park.
No formal notification of the protest had been sent to the municipal authorities.
The protesters alleged, inter alia, that the tree felling in Gorky Park was unjustified and not duly authorised, and demanded proof of its legality.
Some protesters actively attempted to interfere with the tree-felling work in Gorky Park by climbing trees with the help of climbing equipment and attaching themselves to the trees to be felled.
Some protesters interfered with work to be carried out by machinery by placing themselves in front of it.
In some instances, clashes took place between security guards and protesters in Gorky Park.

The Guidelines on Freedom of Peaceful Assembly define an assembly as the intentional and temporary presence of a number of individuals in a public place for a common expressive purpose, and state that all types of peaceful assembly deserve protection.

The Guidelines on Freedom of Peaceful Assembly state that the term 'peaceful' should be interpreted to include conduct that may annoy or give offence to persons opposed to the ideas being promoted, and even conduct that temporarily hinders, impedes or obstructs the activities of third parties, and that assemblies involving purely passive resistance should be characterized as peaceful.

One issue raised in connection with the Gorky Park events is whether the arrest and conviction of the first six applicants for refusal to obey orders to leave the construction site breached their freedom of peaceful assembly.
Regarding the arrest and conviction issue, the first five applicants were arrested together, forming one sub-group.
Regarding the arrest and conviction issue, the sixth applicant was arrested on a different date from the first five applicants, forming a separate sub-group.
On 28 May 2010 the first to fifth, the eighth and the tenth applicants, among other protesters, were arrested and taken to a police station.

At the police station on 28 May 2010, charges of malicious insubordination in the face of lawful demands of a police officer were drawn up against the first to fifth, the eighth and the tenth applicants.
At the close of the hearing on 9 June 2010 the Kharkiv Dzerzhinsky District Court convicted the first and second applicants as charged and sentenced them to fifteen days' administrative detention.
The Kharkiv Dzerzhinsky District Court's decision convicting the first and second applicants was enforced immediately and the applicants were taken into custody.
On 14 June 2010 the Kharkiv Dzerzhinsky District Court, having heard the police officers, the third and fourth applicants and some witnesses, convicted the third and fourth applicants as charged.

On 23 June 2010 the Kharkiv Dzerzhinsky District Court, having heard the police officers, the fifth applicant and some witnesses, convicted the fifth applicant as charged and fined him 170 Ukrainian hryvnias (UAH), at the time the equivalent of about 17 euros (EUR).
On 6 July 2010 the sixth applicant was arrested and charged with malicious insubordination in the face of orders given by police officers to leave the construction site in Gorky Park.
On 7 July 2010 the Kharkiv Dzerzhinsky District Court convicted the sixth applicant as charged and sentenced him to ten days' administrative detention.

Article 39 of the Constitution of Ukraine provides that citizens have the right to assemble peacefully without arms and to hold meetings, rallies, processions and demonstrations, upon notifying in advance the bodies of executive power or bodies of local self-government.

Article 39 of the Constitution of Ukraine provides that restrictions on the exercise of the right to peaceful assembly may be established by a court in accordance with the law and only in the interests of national security and public order, with the purpose of preventing disturbances or crimes, protecting the health of the population, or protecting the rights and freedoms of other persons.

Article 32 § 1 of the Code of Administrative Offences of 1984 provides that administrative detention for up to fifteen days may be applied by courts only in exceptional cases for certain administrative offences.

Article 185 of the Code of Administrative Offences of 1984 provides that malicious disobedience in the face of a lawful order or demand by a police officer who is carrying out his official duties shall be punished by a fine of between 136 and 255 Ukrainian hryvnias (UAH), or by withholding 20% of earnings; or, in the event that in the particular circumstances of the case and with regard to the offender's character these measures are found to be insufficient, by administrative detention of up to fifteen days.

Article 185-1 of the Code of Administrative Offences of 1984 provides that a breach of the procedure for organising and holding meetings, rallies, street marches and demonstrations shall be punishable by a reprimand or by a fine, and that the same actions committed within a year of the application of administrative penalties or by the organiser shall be punishable by a fine, or by correctional labour of one to two months with a deduction of 20% of earnings, or by administrative detention of up to fifteen days.

Under Article 294 of the Code of Administrative Offences of 1984, the parties to administrative-offence proceedings have the right to appeal against court judgments within ten days of their delivery, and such an appeal is to be submitted through the court of first instance.

Under Article 294 of the Code of Administrative Offences of 1984, the court of first instance must, within three days, refer the appeal together with the case file to a court of appeal, which has twenty days to examine the case.

Under Article 294 of the Code of Administrative Offences of 1984, the court of appeal must notify the parties about the hearing not later than three days before the hearing, and the failure of parties to appear does not prevent the court from examining the case, except where a good reason is shown for their failure to appear or the court has no information that the party failing to appear has been duly notified.
Rule 1.16 of Construction Norms and Rules III-4-80 prohibited access of unauthorised persons to construction sites.

The Kharkiv city police action plan of 19 May 2010 mentioned that the tree felling could potentially generate picketing, demonstrations and other unexpected action by opponents of the construction project.

According to the decision of 9 August 2010, the Municipal Guard (MG) staff had asked individuals who were within the perimeter to leave the area in order to avoid the risk of trauma from the construction equipment, and when they refused, the Main Contractor's management had appealed to the police for help in removing those individuals from the construction site.

Article 185 of the Code of Administrative Offences of 1984 provides that malicious disobedience in the face of a lawful order or demand by a police officer who is carrying out his official duties shall be punished by a fine of between 136 and 255 Ukrainian hryvnias (UAH), or by withholding 20% of earnings; or, in the event that in the particular circumstances of the case and with regard to the offender's character these measures are found to be insufficient, by administrative detention of up to fifteen days.
Rule 1.16 of Construction Norms and Rules III-4-80 prohibited access of unauthorised persons to construction sites.
The applicants submitted that the construction site had no boundary markers and they had believed that they were lawfully in a public open space.

Video material for 28 May 2010 shows the individual in civilian clothing repeating several times 'Please leave the construction site', receiving the response 'This is a park, not a construction site'.
At the close of the hearing on 9 June 2010 the Kharkiv Dzerzhinsky District Court convicted the first and second applicants as charged and sentenced them to fifteen days' administrative detention.

The Kharkiv Dzerzhinsky District Court stated that, in view of the examined evidence including that submitted by the defence, it was convinced that the first and second applicants were guilty as charged.

The Kharkiv Dzerzhinsky District Court stated that the video recording submitted by the applicants' lawyer had not exculpated the first and second applicants since it had pauses and did not show certain witnesses, and therefore could not be regarded as a complete record of the events.

The Kharkiv Dzerzhinsky District Court stated that having examined the circumstances of the case and the character of the first and second applicants, it was convinced that a punishment less severe than detention would not be adequate.
The Kharkiv Dzerzhinsky District Court's decision convicting the first and second applicants was enforced immediately and the applicants were taken into custody.

The first and second applicants' lawyer argued on appeal that under the Code of Administrative Offences administrative detention could only be applied in exceptional cases, and that the Kharkiv Dzerzhinsky District Court had failed to explain the exceptional nature of the applicants' cases which would justify the severity of the punishment imposed.

The Kharkiv Regional Court of Appeal concluded that the Kharkiv Dzerzhinsky District Court had not had sufficient grounds to impose the maximum punishment on the first and second applicants, having failed to sufficiently take into account the circumstances of the cases and the applicants' personal characteristics.
The Kharkiv Regional Court of Appeal reduced the first and second applicants' sentence from fifteen days to nine days' detention.

In his appeal the third applicant argued that he could not be held liable for failure to comply with the order of the police since he had had the right to be present in Gorky Park and the order to leave it had been without legal basis.

On 27 July 2010 the Kharkiv Regional Court of Appeal quashed the fifth applicant's conviction by a final decision and discontinued the proceedings against the fifth applicant under Article 22 of the Code of Administrative Offences of 1984.

The Kharkiv Regional Court of Appeal found that the trial court had correctly established the facts concerning the fifth applicant's guilt, but that its judgment lacked reasoning as to the degree of dangerousness of the applicant's conduct and his personal characteristics.

The Kharkiv Regional Court of Appeal found it established that the fifth applicant's registered residence was in Kharkiv, that he was employed and that his actions had not caused prejudice to the public interest or to individuals.

The Kharkiv Regional Court of Appeal found that the delinquent element in the fifth applicant's conduct had been so insignificant that an oral reprimand would have sufficed under Article 22 of the Code of Administrative Offences of 1984, and proceeded to issue the reprimand.
On 8 June 2010 the Kharkiv Dzerzhinsky District Court discontinued proceedings against the eighth applicant.
On 12 July 2010 the Kharkiv Dzerzhinsky District Court discontinued proceedings against the tenth applicant.

In its judgment concerning the eighth applicant, the Kharkiv Dzerzhinsky District Court noted that his explanations were consistent with a private video recording of the events submitted by him, and that there were inconsistencies between various police reports in the case file and a lack of evidence that the officers had duly instructed him to leave.

Concerning the tenth applicant, the Kharkiv Dzerzhinsky District Court likewise pointed to inconsistencies between various police reports in the case file and the lack of evidence that the officers had duly instructed him to leave.
At the hearing on 7 July 2010 the sixth applicant acknowledged that he had been sitting on the ground in the construction area, protesting against the tree felling, which he considered unlawful.

The sixth applicant acknowledged that he had refused to comply with the police officers' requests to leave the construction site, to the point where they had had to drag him away by the arms with his legs dragging on the ground.
The sixth applicant admitted that he had told the police officers that he would return to the construction site as soon as he could.
On 7 July 2010 the Kharkiv Dzerzhinsky District Court convicted the sixth applicant as charged and sentenced him to ten days' administrative detention.

In justifying the sanction imposed on the sixth applicant, the Kharkiv Dzerzhinsky District Court stated that it had taken into account the nature of the offence and its specific circumstances, the applicant's personal characteristics, the fact that he had no employment, the absence of aggravating or attenuating circumstances, and the need to re-educate the offender and to prevent new offences.

The Kharkiv Dzerzhinsky District Court considered that the use of sanctions less severe than imprisonment would be insufficient and that administrative detention needed to be imposed on the sixth applicant, but not for the maximum duration provided for in the law.

Article 32 § 1 of the Code of Administrative Offences of 1984 provides that administrative detention for up to fifteen days may be applied by courts only in exceptional cases for certain administrative offences.

Article 185 of the Code of Administrative Offences of 1984 provides that malicious disobedience in the face of a lawful order or demand by a police officer who is carrying out his official duties shall be punished by a fine of between 136 and 255 Ukrainian hryvnias (UAH), or by withholding 20% of earnings; or, in the event that in the particular circumstances of the case and with regard to the offender's character these measures are found to be insufficient, by administrative detention of up to fifteen days.

The Guidelines on Freedom of Peaceful Assembly provide that law enforcement officers should allow time for people in a crowd to respond as individuals to the situation they face, including any warnings or directions given to them.

The Guidelines on Freedom of Peaceful Assembly provide that if dispersal is deemed necessary, the assembly organiser and participants should be clearly and audibly informed prior to any intervention by law enforcement personnel, and should be given reasonable time to disperse voluntarily, and only if participants then fail to disperse may law enforcement officials intervene further.

Amnesty International's letter of 17 June 2010 stated that at about 6 a.m. on 28 May 2010 a large number of Municipal Guard security guards started to break up the human chain formed by the demonstrators in Gorky Park, and were joined after a few minutes by police officers who then detained 10-12 people and took them to the Dzerzhinsky district police station.

Amnesty International's letter of 17 June 2010 stated that witnesses reported that at no point during the events of 28 May 2010 did the police officers make any requests or demands to the demonstrators that might have resulted in the charges against Andrei Yevarnitsky and Denis Chernega.
The police officers deployed at the Gorky Park construction site allegedly remained largely passive in the face of the clashes between security guards and protesters.
According to the seventh applicant, police officers who were standing nearby on 31 May 2010 observed the assault on her without reacting to her cries for help.

On various dates the protesters, including some of the applicants, complained to the law-enforcement authorities that they had been assaulted by unidentified loggers and men in black clothing with Municipal Guard (MG) badges.
The protesters' complaints to law-enforcement authorities also alleged that the police officers stationed nearby had done nothing to protect them during the Gorky Park events.
The protesters' complaints were investigated by the Kharkiv city prosecutor's office.
On 24 June 2010 the Kharkiv city prosecutor's office decided not to institute any criminal proceedings.
On 4 August 2010 the Kharkiv regional prosecutor's office overruled the Kharkiv city prosecutor's office decision of 24 June 2010 not to institute criminal proceedings and ordered a further inquiry.

Following an additional round of pre-investigation enquiries, on 9 August 2010 the Kharkiv city prosecutor's office decided not to institute criminal proceedings against loggers A. and K., managers of the Main Contractor and subcontractor companies, Municipal Guard (MG), the Kharkiv City Council or its executive authorities, including the Kharkiv Municipal Construction Department, for lack of constituent elements of a crime in their actions.
On 13 August 2010 the police refused to institute criminal proceedings in connection with the seventh applicant's complaint of ill-treatment.

On 20 March 2012 the Kharkiv Dzerzhinsky District Court quashed the police decision of 13 August 2010 on the grounds that the requirements of the Code of Criminal Procedure of 1960 concerning pre-investigation enquiries had not been complied with and the seventh applicant's allegations had not been verified.

The applicants submitted a copy of a letter from their lawyer to the district police dated 3 October 2014, stating that after the Kharkiv Dzerzhinsky District Court's decision of 20 March 2012, the seventh applicant had not been informed about any further progress in the proceedings.

On 31 July 2014, in response to the Court's request for further observations, the Government informed the Court that material concerning enquiries into the seventh and ninth applicants' allegations of ill-treatment had been destroyed due to the expiry of the time-limit for their preservation.
The Government provided a statement documenting the destruction of the material concerning enquiries into the seventh and ninth applicants' allegations of ill-treatment, dated 9 September 2013.

In November 2010 a number of protesters, including all the applicants, lodged an action with the Kharkiv Circuit Administrative Court, complaining that the police had failed to protect them against assaults during their peaceful protest against the tree felling, in particular on 28 and 31 May and 1 and 2 June 2010.
On 24 May 2011 the Kharkiv Circuit Administrative Court rejected the applicants' claim that the police had failed to protect them against assaults during their protest.

On 26 June 2014 the High Administrative Court allowed an appeal lodged by the applicants and remitted the case to the Kharkiv Circuit Administrative Court for re-examination on the grounds that the lower courts' examination of the facts had been incomplete.

The High Administrative Court found that the lower courts had failed, in particular, to establish whether attacks on the protesters had really taken place, the list of the officers present, and whether the protesters had appealed for help.

The Guidelines on Freedom of Peaceful Assembly provide that the policing of assemblies must be guided by the human rights principles of legality, necessity, proportionality and non-discrimination, and that the State has a positive duty to take reasonable and appropriate measures to enable peaceful assemblies to take place without participants fearing physical violence.

The Guidelines on Freedom of Peaceful Assembly provide that law enforcement officials must protect participants of a peaceful assembly from any person or group that attempts to disrupt or inhibit it in any way.

The Guidelines on Freedom of Peaceful Assembly provide that law-enforcement officials should be liable for any failure to fulfil their positive obligations to protect and facilitate the right to freedom of peaceful assembly, and that liability should also extend to private agencies or individuals acting on behalf of the state.
